title: Chapter 4: The Middle of the Rope
blurb: The key-eaters lose their dispute but win Ravi a deeper culprit, and the pipe's real tenant has already filed a complaint against him.

blocks.text: Floor 5 had a notice board. I'd walked past it every night I'd been up there and taken it for something nobody had got round to taking down: green baize in an oak frame by the lift doors, brass drawing pins gone brown, nothing on it. Tonight it had two papers.

One was mine, a carbon of WO-5-002, the third copy, the one I'd never known what was for, with my own handwriting slanting across the cause line. The other was smaller, and its letters hadn't been written. They'd been bitten: tiny capitals nibbled right through the paper, so the green showed behind every one.
RULING AT MIDNIGHT, said the bottom line.
"Served party disputes cause," Mrs Wrobel said over my shoulder, before her eyes had got anywhere near it. "Both claims posted. Building rules at midnight."
Then she leaned in and actually read it, and stopped talking.
Kit had asked me which way the fifth floor was the afternoon before, at the kerb, with the parcel in one hand and the phone in the other, and I had answered with the lift.

"It's a goods lift," I said. "Round the back, off the service corridor. Works on a key. The plate says four people and a dog, and honestly I wouldn't put four in it. The cable's older than both of us put together, and the gate sticks unless you lift it as you pull."
"That's not a direction," Kit said.
"I'm telling you where the lift is."

"You're telling me how heavy it is." Kit looked up at the roofline again, then at me, then at my hands, which were still curled round an empty coffee cup because that was the shape they'd set in. "Label says fifth floor. Building says four. App says service lift. You say the lift's got a weight limit. Somebody's lying, and the building's brick, so."
"Leave it by the lift," I said. "The doors at the back. I'll see it's..." I didn't know what I'd see it was. "I'll see to it."

Kit wheeled the bike down the side passage, narrating under their breath (left at the bins, mind the drain, door with the wired glass), and set the parcel on the tiles in front of the service-lift doors, square to them, the way you'd leave something for someone who'd told you exactly where they'd be. Then they photographed it for the app. Dusty had followed us down the passage and sat by the bins, watching the parcel.
"Eleven months I've been on unlisted," Kit said, "and I've never once had a door I couldn't find. Two stars."
"It was three ten minutes ago."
"It was three before you started on about cables." The helmet went back on. The owl on it gave me a long look. "Docked one for the lying. Nothing personal. Your step's still a trap."

I didn't open the parcel. It wasn't addressed to me, and I couldn't have got under that tape with my fingers the way they were. I read the label twice and left it where Kit had put it, and every time I passed it that night it was still there, waiting for whoever lived behind a door I'd signed for and couldn't yet open.

The next evening the Works Book was lying open on the office desk when I came down at nine, which I'd stopped expecting anything else of. It had turned itself to floor 5. My order had grown a line at the bottom, in the copperplate that wasn't mine.

``` WO-5-002            FLOOR 5            TIER 1 FAULT:      RISER 2, JOINTS FAILING. LEAK. PEST PASSAGE TO FLOORS 1-4. CAUSE:      key-eaters nesting at foot of riser 2 chase, gnawing the joints. SERVED ON:  the key-eaters, riser 2, floor 5. GRADE REQUIRED: 1 STATUS:     TRANSFERRED. DISPUTED. NOTICE:     FLOOR 5 BOARD. RULING AT MIDNIGHT. ```

I read it twice, lips going, turning the page flat with the heel of my hand because my fingers wouldn't pinch, and DISPUTED didn't get any friendlier the second time. I'd been disputed on site before. A roofer once spent a fortnight telling a client that a split valley gutter was down to me and not his boots, and what I took from that was that whoever did the damage always has a story about why it wasn't really him. The teeth were in the joints. I'd had my thumb in the marks.
Dusty had followed me down and was lying across the office doorway with his chin on his paws.
"They're arguing it," I told him. "Can you argue with a pipe? I didn't know you could argue with a pipe. I've been trying for years."
He sighed through his nose, which is what he does in the office instead of answering.

When I went through to the service corridor at half ten, Mrs Wrobel was standing by the lift doors in her outdoor coat, with a paper bag in one hand and her Yale on its string round her neck. Kit's parcel was at her feet. She'd read the label; I could tell by the way she wasn't looking at it.
"I am coming up," she said.
"It's a maintenance lift. There's a weight limit."
"I weigh fifty kilos, and you weigh nothing, because you don't eat. Key, Mr Caretaker."
There was a birthday card sticking out of her coat pocket, stamped and addressed in square capitals to somewhere out past the estuary. I said she'd missed the last post.
"It is for my sister. Seventy-five on Saturday. She wants the whole family there, overnight, with a cake from a shop."
"You should go. I'll keep an eye on 4C."
"No," she said, and that was the whole of it. She pushed the card down into her pocket until it was gone.

I thought of the brown coat and the slippers standing just inside her door. Some people don't leave a flat with slippers like that in it, not for a night, not for a cake from a shop. I turned the lift key with the side of my hand, because my fingers wouldn't grip it, and the gate took two goes.

In the cage she went straight to the back corner, away from the gate, and set her palm flat on the wall panel, the way you'd hold a rail you'd held before. I pressed 5 with my knuckle. The glass bead lit. She watched it light and said nothing about it at all.

When the doors opened she stepped out onto the brown lino before I did. She put two fingers on the dado rail and stood there with her eyes shut for about as long as it takes to say a short prayer. I didn't ask. I went and looked at the notice board instead, and that was where she came and found me, and read the papers before she'd read them.
The bitten paper said this, once she'd stopped talking and I'd got close enough to make out the holes:
``` DISPUTE. WO-5-002. WE BIT. WE WERE PUT OUT FIRST. OLD NEST BEHIND THE PANEL. THE WHITE CAME. WE WENT DOWN. WE COUGH NOW. ```

"They're saying they were evicted," I said. "Somebody stuffed the run with that white lagging, years back, and they didn't like it. I've seen it in the bites. I wouldn't like it either." I looked at the last line longer than I meant to. They coughed now because I'd put it on them. "But they still bit the joints."
Mrs Wrobel coughed too, the dry one, into her sleeve. I hadn't coughed in two days and had nearly got used to it.
"Better evidence of cause wins," she said. "Equal evidence, greater standing wins. Standing is how long you are here."
"I've been here four months."
"Yes." She looked at the bitten paper. "They have been in this pipe longer than that."
"I've got the teeth marks," I said. "They're in the caulking. They're in the iron on two of the joints. You could put your thumb in them."
She didn't argue. She opened the paper bag, broke a poppy-seed roll in half and then in half again, put a quarter into my hand and closed my fingers round it for me, as far as they'd close.
"Then you have teeth marks," she said. "Eat."
I ate. I have never once in my life won an argument with someone holding bread.
She asked where the nest was, and I pointed down the corridor towards riser 2's cupboard. She looked that way for a while without moving her feet.
"Take me down," she said. "I am seventy-one and it is late. At midnight you stand here. You don't go anywhere. You read it twice."
I said I always read things twice.
"I know," she said.
I rode her down to four. On the landing she stopped with her hand on her own doorframe and said, "Good night, Mr Caretaker," which was more than I'd had from her at that door for two days.

At ten to midnight Dusty was sitting by the lift doors next to Kit's parcel, as if the two of them had been waiting up together. When I got the gate open with my forearm he walked in ahead of me, the first time he'd ridden since night two, and sat down facing the doors.
"Oh, now you come," I said. "Now there's a ruling. Where've you been all week?"

On floor 5 he got out and stood by the board with me. The bulbs hummed in their bowl shades. Down the corridor riser 2 was dripping, and further off, very faintly, something coughed wetly. I tried not to hear it as my fault, and heard it as my fault.

At midnight by my watch, the ink on both papers moved. It didn't run. It slid, letter by letter, the bitten capitals and my own slanting hand alike, and settled into copperplate the way water finds its level.

``` NOTICE. FLOOR 5. WO-5-002. RISER 2, JOINTS FAILING. SERVICE ON THE KEY-EATERS: STANDS. PARTY HAD A PART IN THE FAULT. DISPUTE: UPHELD. EVIDENCE OF A DEEPER LINK. PARTY DRIVEN FROM ITS NEST. ORDER RETURNS TO SERVER. NO BOUNCE. HOLDER: R. ANAND. MAY SERVE AGAIN. ```
I read it twice. I'd got to RETURNS the second time when the cough came back.

It came all at once, the wet chill and the cough together, and it wasn't the cough I'd carried for five nights. It was that one with another one inside it. I bent over with my hands on my knees and coughed until the bulbs swam. And my hands, which had been bad, went past bad. The knuckles disappeared. My fingers sat on the ends of my palms like they'd been borrowed from a bigger man and blown up for a party.

"Okay," I said to Dusty. "Okay. That's both of them, then. That's me with the riser and the door. Is that allowed? It feels like it shouldn't be allowed. I've been trying to sign for two all week and the pen won't even go on the line, and now it just hands me..."
Dusty walked back into the lift, sat down, and looked at me until I came and stood in the doorway with my shoulder against the door so it stayed open.
"It's allowed," Walter said.
His voice was the same as on night two: gravel, no hurry, a man who'd said all this before to somebody else.

"They did chew it, son. That's why it didn't bounce on you. Put a name on an order that had no hand in the fault, and it bounces. They had a hand. But something put them out of their house and down that pipe, and that something's further down the chain than they are. Deeper link's the better evidence. That's all the board said."
"I had the teeth marks."
"You had the middle of the rope. They showed the board where it was tied."
I coughed. It took a while. "And it's back on me. On top of the door."

"An order that comes back to you off a lost dispute, the book lets you carry past your limit. Doesn't mean your body likes it. While you're over, everything you carry, you carry twice. Doesn't matter how far over. Twice is the worst it does."
"Brilliant," I said. "Good. That's a relief, that is."

"Now listen, because this is the useful bit. It's changed hands. That means you can serve it again. Not on them. On whatever put them out. And whatever that is gets its own go at disputing, same as they did."
"What put them out?"
"Go and look. You'll learn it off the pipe, not off me." He shifted on the lift floor. "And that courier."
"Kit."
"Kit. A slip a courier carries counts as served by whoever sent it, not by the courier. You remember that."
"Why would I need Kit to..."
"Eleven months on runs like today's, the kid said. Eleven months, son. That's a kid who's stood at the back door of every building in this city that's got floors it shouldn't have."
I stood there with the door against my shoulder and the drip going down the corridor. "There are others."
"Go and look at your pipe." Then, as I turned: "One more thing. Anywhere on this floor that's somebody's home, you ask before you go in. Grade nought, grade anything. A home's a home."
"I know that. I'm not going in anybody's flat."
"Good," he said, and put his chin down on his paws, and was a dog again, with the doors still open.

I went to riser 2's cupboard first and opened it and stood in the drip. The joints were weeping all down the run the way they had been for a week, crescent bites in the lead caulking, and in some of the bites the white fluff I'd taken for lagging.
"Sorry," I said to it. "I put the wrong name on you. Not the wrong name. Half a name. I'll find what's really eating you before morning. I promise you that. Before morning."

The droppings I'd followed down the chase on night six had been fresh, black, rice-sized. There were others, once I put the torch low along the skirting: grey and dry, old enough to go to powder when the light touched them, and they went the other way. Away from the chase, back up the corridor, past the doors with enamel numbers. I followed them bent double, coughing into my elbow, telling them what I was doing as I went.
"Just going where you went. Just backwards. Nobody's in trouble. Well. I'm in trouble."

They stopped at a panel in the wall, a little way short of the unnumbered door. The mushroom smell was strong there, which made sense with that door so close. The panel came up to my chest, painted the same tea colour as the wallpaper so you'd miss it, held by four quarter-turn catches. Along its bottom edge the paint was scratched in tiny arcs, over and over, like keys turning in a lock that wasn't there.

No door. No number. No handle. A board over a hole in a wall is what you put over pipes, not over people. That's what a service void is: the pipes' room. Walter had said homes, and the only things that had ever made a home in there had been put out of it and were down at the slab now, coughing. I'd be looking at plant.
I did the catches with the heel of my hand, one after another, and lifted the board away.
"Just the pipes," I told the dark. "Just having a look at the pipes."

Warm air came out, wet, like opening a dishwasher. The void went back further than the wall had any right to, and riser 2 came up through the middle of it, the top of the same run, offsetting through here before it dropped into its cupboard. I'd wondered where the top went.

Everything in there was grey-white. It lay over the walls and the backs of the pipes and the slab like the felt on an old hat, soft and close and thick, and it had grown up the riser and into every joint. Threads like wet wool had gone into the lead and through the oakum and out the other side, and the sockets stood a fraction proud, pushed apart from the inside, every one. You could see the leak start in them. The teeth had come after.

In the corner was the old nest. Keys again, plaited, but older, green with age, and the white had grown through the whole thing, through every bow and every ward. Nobody had lived in it for a long time.
The white came. They went down.
"Oh," I said, and coughed, and said it again. "Oh, it's you. It was always you. That wasn't lagging."
I'd found it. Before morning, with hours to spare. I stood there with the torch shaking because my fingers couldn't hold it still, and felt, for the first time all night, like I knew something.
Then I moved the torch across it, and the whole grey mat shivered, the way a coat on a hook does when someone breathes against it.
I put the board back. I did the catches up with my palm. I didn't run, because you don't run on a floor you're still learning, but I didn't walk slowly either.
It was half past twelve when I got back to the board, and there was a new paper on it.
Its letters hadn't been written or bitten. They'd grown. Grey, soft at the edges, spreading into the paper the way damp comes through a ceiling, and still spreading while I watched.

``` COMPLAINT. FLOOR 5. 00:31. FILED BY:  THE FELT, HEAD TENANT, FLOOR 5. AGAINST:   THE CARETAKER. TRESPASS. CAME IN BY THE PANEL WITHOUT LEAVE. SHONE A LIGHT IN OUR HOME. RULING AT THE NEXT MIDNIGHT. ```
I read it twice. It didn't get any smaller.
"Walter," I said, without turning round. "What's a head tenant?"
From the lift, where a grey dog lay with his chin on his paws and the doors still open, Walter said, "The one you should have knocked for, son."
